articles.text: Each election cycle, the Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage of each candidate to help residents make informed voting decisions. For this year’s race, the Post will send one question per week to the candidates running for City Council until Election Day. The five City Council candidates vying for three open seats received the question on Tuesday, October 6, and were asked to reply in 200 words. Week 7 question: According to Piedmont’s Flock Transparency Portal, Piedmont operates 57 license plate reader cameras and 150 agencies have access to Piedmont’s data. Would you vote to renew the contract with Flock Safety, and what would you do to increase transparency efforts around the program? What limits, if any, would you place on which agencies can access the data? Nancy Beninati (NancyforPiedmont.com) Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) can be a valuable tool for law enforcement to investigate and identify vehicles involved in criminal activity. But technology that collects information about people moving through our community requires appropriate oversight, accountability, and transparency. Recently, the San Francisco Police Department (SFPD) revealed its ALPR data was accessed by out-of-state and federal agencies contrary to state law and without SFPD’s permission. When SFPD officials raised the issue with Flock, a private company, they found the response unsatisfactory. A related issue arose in Richmond. These examples underscore that even when steps are taken to protect the information, oversight is necessary. I have reviewed Piedmont’s ALPR policy. Given recent concerns about ALPR technology and Flock specifically, there should be a community discussion to consider whether our policy needs updating and to ensure our daily movements are protected. Piedmonters should understand how these systems are used, who can access the data and under what circumstances, and what protections exist against misuse. Mandatory audits must be thorough. articles.text: Editor: We seek your assistance in making sure that Piedmont Firefighters are accorded salaries and health benefits in keeping with the fact that they are our Piedmont citizens’ extended family in terms of their dedication to our health and safety. We moved to Piedmont in 1993 and raised our two children here. We have experienced the intelligence, caring and decision-making of our Piedmont Firefighters. Had we not personally benefited from the firefighters’ kindness and skill, we would still feel tremendous gratitude to them for being here just in case. We were very distressed to read the article in the September 23 Piedmont Post indicating that negotiations between the firefighters and the city are at a standstill. We carefully read the firefighters’ concerns about the necessity of 1) having pay increases to encourage longevity, and 2) having retirement benefits to cover firefighters’ medical care for the period between retirement and Social Security eligibility. We share the firefighters’ underlying concern about inadequate staffing which requires excessive overtime to keep us safe. As residents and taxpayers, we support the firefighters’ demands. Piedmont prides itself on being a city that is at the forefront of good decision-making. Piedmont needs to step up to support the firefighters and to inform its citizens what efforts and finances are required to do so. We rely on Piedmont Firefighters for our lives and the lives of our children. Is there anything more important? The firefighters’ knowledge, skills, courage and work ethic should be celebrated and honored by accepting their demands. We are both retired attorneys; Joe represented injured workers and clients denied social security disability; I practiced civil rights law. As residents of Piedmont, we find the city’s response puzzling and extraordinarily short-sighted (using overtime instead of properly hiring, making the very hiring process discouraging by not providing the enticement of raises after certain years of service are reached, by not meeting the basic human need of health insurance until Social Security eligibility is reached). We look forward to hearing from you. –Susan Goldsmith and Joseph Waxman
articles.title: City needs to fix hiring procedure at Fire Dept.

articles.text: Editor, My family recently bought a home in Piedmont, and my husband and I will be voting yes on Measure GG. We chose Piedmont because of the quality of services the city provides from parks and pool to well-maintained roads and sidewalks and reliable police and fire services. Measure GG would increase the real estate transfer tax, a line item we shared with our home’s seller, to help fund city operations and maintain the services that drew our family here. As recent buyers, we can say that an additional one-time cost as represented by Measure GG would not have changed our decision to purchase a home in Piedmont. The quality of city services was a much more significant factor in our decision. Looking ahead, I am concerned that an inability to maintain these important city services could diminish the qualities that make Piedmont an attractive place to live. –Katy Morsony

articles.text: Editor, Fiscal stewardship is about public trust. How we manage public money shapes both the strength of our institutions and the trust our communities place in them. Peralta’s colleges play an indispensable role in the educational and economic landscape of Alameda County. Peralta expands educational opportunity close to home — giving Piedmont High students access to Calculus III and Linear Algebra classes though Peralta’s Dual and Concurrent enrollment — creating affordable pathways to leading universities, helping adults prepare for new careers, or cultivating art and language skills. By reducing financial barriers and providing opportunities at different stages of life, the Colleges close gaps to access to higher education and economic mobility. Peralta directly shapes the opportunities available to families throughout Northern Alameda county. When Cindi Reiss was first elected to the Peralta Community College District Board in 2018, the District faced serious financial instability, accreditation concerns, persistent leadership turnover, Board conflict, and the possibility of state intervention. Cindi brought to the Board the teaching perspective of a longtime tenured educator, the institutional insight of a former Accreditation Commissioner, and the governance and policy experience gained through local and statewide academic senate service. It is this unique lens that shaped her commitment to responsible fiscal governance. The progress since 2018 is substantial: All four Peralta colleges are fully accredited. In 2026, a successful bond-refunding transaction saved taxpayers $52M. In 2026, Fitch assigned Peralta’s new generalobligation bonds a AAA rating, while S&P assigned an AA-/Stable rating. The rating agencies cited improved financial practices, experienced management, stable Board leadership, and a forwardlooking plan for long-term financial stability. Board leadership matters. Cindi understands that a trustee’s responsibility is not to pursue the easiest or most immediately popular course. It is to shape and protect the long-term fiscal and structural conditions that will allow Peralta to succeed and serve its students effectively even amidst declining enrollments and growing doubts about the value of higher education. Peralta has moved from crisis toward stability, but stability is not the same as sustainability. The District must now implement its Transformation Plan, reduce unnecessary fragmentation and internal competition, strengthen educational pathways, and establish a financial structure that will endure beyond the tenure of any individual trustee or chancellor. I support her reelection because Peralta needs her continued experience, institutional knowledge, independence, and principled stewardship to bring this work to completion. Please join me in voting to reelect Cindi Reiss as Peralta Community College District Trustee, Area 5, on November 3. –Melissa Wilk You may now subscribe online at:

articles.text: Dear Editor, As we head towards the home stretch of the upcoming November 3rd election, and for those who have not yet decided, let me share with you my thoughts of why I support Measure GG. As you may be aware, the City of Piedmont’s annual budget is heavily dependent on real estaterelated taxes, including transfer taxes, which account for about 10% of the City’s General Fund budget. The transfer tax, which is assessed only when one’s Piedmont property is sold, has not changed since 1993. One good year of transfer taxes does not change the structure of the City’s annual budget. At the City Council’s direction, the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning (BAFP) committee explored options in addressing the City’s long-term fiscal needs of maintaining its services and addressing its aging facilities and infrastructure. As one who was instrumental in the establishment of the BAFP committee, it is an open and transparent budget and planning process with all hearings open to the public. BAFP has a longterm view in the planning process and strongly recommended an increase in the City’s transfer tax rate to 1.75% of the sales price, which is within the range of other Alameda County cities. If passed, Measure GG will generate an estimated $1.5 million per year to support general City services. Please join me in supporting Measure GG. –John Chiang, former Piedmont Mayor
articles.title: For Measure GG

Piedmont has great schools, safe streets, fast emergency response, and a strong sense of community. It’s easy to assume a city like ours has vast financial resources. I assumed that too before joining the committee. In reality, our city’s budget is more constrained than many residents realize. Piedmont is almost entirely residential, so nearly all of our revenue comes from property: property taxes, the parcel tax, and the transfer tax paid when a home sells. Meanwhile, most nearby cities benefit from much larger commercial and industrial tax bases. Without that kind of tax revenue, Piedmont depends on the transfer tax in a way our neighbors simply don’t. Our 1.3% transfer tax rate was set 33 years ago and hasn’t changed since, while the city’s costs for salaries, pensions, insurance and construction have kept rising. Over the same period, most of our neighbors have raised their rates, several of them since 2018. pages.text: Wednesday, October 14, 2026 3 LETTERS - MAIN Support Measure GG Editor, My family recently bought a home in Piedmont, and my husband and I will be voting yes on Measure GG. We chose Piedmont because of the quality of services the city provides from parks and pool to well-maintained roads and sidewalks and reliable police and fire services. Measure GG would increase the real estate transfer tax, a line item we shared with our home’s seller, to help fund city operations and maintain the services that drew our family here. As recent buyers, we can say that an additional one-time cost as represented by Measure GG would not have changed our decision to purchase a home in Piedmont. The quality of city services was a much more significant factor in our decision. Looking ahead, I am concerned that an inability to maintain these important city services could diminish the qualities that make Piedmont an attractive place to live. –Katy Morsony interest rates and the economy, and a strong year doesn’t fix the longterm gap between what the city needs to maintain and what it can count on. Measure GG bolsters a one-time tax paid at the time of sale, and it addresses a real need I’ve seen firsthand. I hope you’ll join me in voting yes. –Billy Deitch is a Piedmont resident and member of the city’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee. Views are his own. Why I’m Voting Yes on Measure GG Editor, Serving on Piedmont’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee has taught me a lot about how our city’s finances work, and it’s why I support Measure GG to increase the real estate transfer tax rate. Piedmont has great schools, safe streets, fast emergency response, and a strong sense of community. It’s easy to assume a city like ours has vast financial resources. I assumed that too before joining the committee. In reality, our city’s budget is more constrained than many residents realize. Piedmont is almost entirely residential, so nearly all of our revenue comes from property: property taxes, the parcel tax, and the transfer tax paid when a home sells. Meanwhile, most nearby cities benefit from much larger commercial and industrial tax bases. Without that kind of tax revenue, Piedmont depends on the transfer tax in a way our neighbors simply don’t. Our 1.3% transfer tax rate was set 33 years ago and hasn’t changed since, while the city’s costs for salaries, pensions, insurance and construction have kept rising. Over the same period, most of our neighbors have raised their rates, several of them since 2018. At the average Piedmont home price, our current rate is lower than Berkeley’s, Oak land’s, Emer y ville’s or Albany’s. Measure GG would raise it to 1.75%, ge ne r at i ng a b out $1.5 million a year for police, fire, and maintenance of our roads, storm drains, parks and city buildings. Transfer tax revenue does go up when home sales are strong, and we’ve had some good years. But sales rise and fall with For Measure GG Dear Editor, As we head towards the home stretch of the upcoming November 3rd election, and for those who have not yet decided, let me share with you my thoughts of why I support Measure GG. As you may be aware, the City of Piedmont’s annual budget is heavily dependent on real estaterelated taxes, including transfer taxes, which account for about 10% of the City’s General Fund budget. The transfer tax, which is assessed only when one’s Piedmont property is sold, has not changed since 1993. One good year of transfer taxes does not change the structure of the City’s annual budget. At the City Council’s direction, the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning (BAFP) committee explored options in addressing the City’s long-term fiscal needs of maintaining its services and addressing its aging facilities and infrastructure. BAFP has a longterm view in the planning process and strongly recommended an increase in the City’s transfer tax rate to 1.75% of the sales price, which is within the range of other Alameda County cities. Couldn’t we reimagine our heart of downtown as not just Mulberry’s, but also a vibrant town square with family-friendly businesses (e.g. pizza, ice cream shops)? Might we use the solid foundation inherited from previous City Councils, to accelerate progress infused with fresh views from a young Piedmont dad with a decade-plus of private sector leadership credentials? Adam’s most compelling ideas revolve around exploring new revenue opportunities and public-private partnerships to help take our community to the next level – not just for young families, but for all of us Piedmonters. I’ve had the great privilege of working with Tom for 4 years on Piedmont’s Planning Commission. During that time, and throughout his tenure on City Council, I’ve been deeply impressed by Tom’s approach to understanding complex issues and making thoughtful decisions. Tom emphasizes collaboration and cooperation between neighbors, and balances maintaining the character of the community with being open to design innovation. This approach was reflected in his exceptional leadership in revising Piedmont’s Design Guidelines. His efforts have made the Design Guidelines more transparent and user-friendly for homeowners, architects and contractors alike. Tom’s many years of engagement and service in Piedmont reflect his dedication to our community. Tom’s professional expertise as an architect and executive has been extraordinarily helpful to City Council as Piedmont completed construction on its new pool and moves forward with complying with state housing laws. Finally, Tom’s warm, collegial, and solutions-focused nature ensures that different viewpoints are respected and reflected in the Council’s decisions on important issues facing our city. I look forward to electing Tom Ramsey to City Council. I hope you’ll join me in casting your ballot for him in November. –Rani Batra, Former Chair, Piedmont Planning Commission Re-Elect Cindi Reiss for Peralta Community College Board Trustee, Area 5 Editor, Fiscal stewardship is about public trust. How we manage public money shapes both the strength of our institutions and the trust our communities place in them. Peralta’s colleges play an indispensable role in the educational and economic landscape of Alameda County. Peralta expands educational opportunity close to home — giving Piedmont High students access to Calculus III and Linear Algebra classes though Peralta’s Dual and Concurrent enrollment — creating affordable pathways to leading universities, helping adults prepare for new careers, or cultivating art and language skills. By reducing financial barriers and providing opportunities at different stages of life, the Colleges close gaps to access to higher education and economic mobility. Peralta directly shapes the opportunities available to families throughout Northern Alameda county. When Cindi Reiss was first elected to the Peralta Community College District Board in 2018, the District faced serious financial instability, accreditation concerns, persistent leadership turnover, Board conflict, and the possibility of state intervention. Cindi brought to the Board the teaching perspective of a longtime tenured educator, the institutional insight of a former Accreditation Commissioner, and the governance and policy experience gained through local and statewide academic senate service. It is this unique lens that shaped her commitment to responsible fiscal governance. The progress since 2018 is substantial: All four Peralta colleges are fully accredited. In 2026, a successful bond-refunding transaction saved taxpayers $52M. In 2026, Fitch assigned Peralta’s new generalobligation bonds a AAA rating, while S&P assigned an AA-/Stable rating. The rating agencies cited improved financial practices, experienced management, stable Board leadership, and a forwardlooking plan for long-term financial stability. Board leadership matters. Cindi understands that a trustee’s responsibility is not to pursue the easiest or most immediately popular course. It is to shape and protect the long-term fiscal and structural conditions that will allow Peralta to succeed and serve its students effectively even amidst declining enrollments and growing doubts about the value of higher education. Peralta has moved from crisis toward stability, but stability is not the same as sustainability. The District must now implement its Transformation Plan, reduce unnecessary fragmentation and internal competition, strengthen educational pathways, and establish a financial structure that will endure beyond the tenure of any individual trustee or chancellor. I support her reelection because Peralta needs her continued experience, institutional knowledge, independence, and principled stewardship to bring this work to completion. articles.text: At the October 5 City Council meeting, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan presented a proposed countywide framework for community protective actions and fire department readiness when the National Weather Service (NWS) forecasts extreme fire weather. The proposal would designate “Leave Early” zones where, under “particularly dangerous” weather conditions, residents would be notified in advance to leave early in case of a wildfire. The NWS typically issues a Red Flag Warning up to 24 hours before hazardous fire weather begins, often preceded by a Fire Weather Watch 24 to 72 hours in advance. Under this proposed framework, the NWS would add a Particularly Dangerous Situation tag to the red flag warnings that meet the weather conditions. “One of the complaints that I personally had, and a lot of the fire service had, was calling red flag on days that don’t do a lot of bad things in terms of fire behavior, and the fires that we have the most trouble with containing happen in very low humidity and very high winds. That caught their attention, and they’ve been engaged ever since,” said Chief Brannigan. The weather conditions that trigger a Particularly Dangerous tag are very rare. According to the report, they have less than a five percent chance of occurring. The conditions are: no rain for the past 24 hours, annual grasses have cured, extremely low humidity, and high wind speeds sustained for more than 8 hours or longer. Under these specific conditions, the NWS would notify the region of a Particularly Dangerous Situation 24 to 48 hours in advance. This drafted approach takes inspiration from Australia’s approach to fire communication. Under catastrophic weather conditions, they would notify people in high-risk areas to leave early before the conditions become dangerous. “On these rare, very extreme weather days, we are proposing creating what we call leave early areas. Now these will be areas that we, as a community, decide where it makes sense to do this,” said Chief Brannigan. Within designated high-risk zones, there will be two categories: “Leave Early” areas and “Get Ready” areas. A Leave Early area would recommend residents leave their home and stay elsewhere before the extreme fire weather window begins and wait until conditions improve. A Get Ready designation recommends residents be ready to evacuate quickly and prepare an evacuation plan in case the situation gets worse. “Whenever we firm up the plan, decide as a community where these areas are in Piedmont, how they line up with our surrounding communities. We will take a really intentional approach to community education and messaging beforehand, so that when it happens, we’re able to send out messaging coordinated,” said Chief Brannigan. Over the next three months, the Alameda County Fire Chiefs Association intends to refine the approach, identify additional support tools, identify partners not yet involved, and identify any legislative changes that may be needed. The association plans to return a final draft for adoption by January 2027 for use in the 2027 fire season. 3. HOLD ON until shaking stops. articles.text: The moment you arrive home, an affectionate head presses against your legs. Vibrant green eyes gaze up at you, and you smile at a small, inquisitive chirp. Meet Marvin: a 5-year-old friend who wants you to be part of his day! This sleek, black cat will follow you around, nap nearby, and occasionally sit in your lap. He enjoys his meals with you by his side, and when he wants attention, he simply sits, watches, and wills you to notice him. Marvin is positive for FIV, a condition easily managed with indoor living and routine veterinary care. This sweet boy occasionally nips when he’s bored, overly excited, or in new situations — so he’ll do well with an adopter who can notice when he’s starting to feel antsy and redirect his energy to toys, keeping his little mind busy with daily playtime. Adopt Marvin through Cat Town. You’ll delight at seeing him scamper enthusiastically after his favorite wand toys and prance anything that rolls — from springs and fuzzy balls to blueberries. articles.text: Refreshing earthquake safety knowledge Pause what you’re doing at 10:15 a.m. on Thursday, October 15, to practice what to do during an earthquake as part of the annual Great California ShakeOut. The Fire Department wants to understand how prepared the community is, what steps residents have taken, where they’re vulnerable, and what might help them be more ready. Complete the City’s disaster preparedness survey at piedmont. ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. Answers will help identify where residents need more support and guide future programs and resources. If you were taught to stand in a doorway when the ground starts shaking, it’s time for a refresher. When the city quizzed residents at this year’s Harvest Festival about what to do during an earthquake, most people gave that answer. Doorways don’t protect against falling or flying objects, one of the most common causes of earthquake injuries. Instead, experts today recommend drop, cover, and hold on. Anytime you feel shaking or get an earthquake alert, take these three steps immediately if you are able: 1. DROP to your hands and knees. This helps protect you from being knocked down by shaking. 2. COVER your head and neck. Crawl under a sturdy desk or table if one is nearby. If not, crawl next to an interior wall and use your arms to protect your head and neck.

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont invites its members and community members to join political scientist and author Seth Masket for a special fundraising luncheon at the Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue on Friday, October 30, at 11:30 a.m. His topic is: “Winning and Losing: How Do Our American Political Parties Remember and Forget?” Piedmont Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen will introduce the speaker. Masket, a University of Denver Professor, will shine a light on some of the surprising differences between how our political parties deal with losses and fight for survival. Appealing to voters of all parties, this talk by a leading scholar will raise important questions and point out intriguing dynamics about party identity, and how parties and their voters deal with wins and losses and hopes for the future. Through interviews with party leaders, insiders, and voters reveals insights and contradictions in how our country’s two main parties operate. His just-published book (June 2026), The Elephants in the Room: How Trump Voters Seized the Party from Republican Leaders, and prior volume (2020), Learning from Loss: The Democrats 2016-2020, provide unique–and remarkable–insights. With his dry sense of humor, he’ll help answer the very timely question: How did we get here? “Seth Masket’s work allows us to step back from the daily political news cycle and examine how political parties actually work,” said Lisa Gardner, President of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont. “For the League, informed and engaged citizens are essential to a healthy democracy. We hope this luncheon will encourage thoughtful conversation and greater understanding of the forces shaping our political system.” Tickets are $40 for LWVP members and $45 for nonmembers. Additional event information is available through the League of Women Voters of Piedmont. Pre-registration is required. Get tickets at: https://bit.ly/4zsxRpB.

articles.text: Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee announced on Monday, October 5 that Children’s Fairyland has secured a $5,000,000 allocation from the state of California to close out phase one of its capital investment in the park. The funds are designed to facilitate the initial stages of restoration and revitalization. “It’s really a storybook that comes to life. Regardless of how old you are or young you are, my family can attest to the fact, this is a dream come true,” said Lee. Children’s Fairyland CEO Kymberly Miller described details of the funding: $3,000,000 will be designated to the park’s capital investment to make sure the park is well cared for in the next 76 years. The remaining $2 million will go to the park’s general operations. The funds come from the state’s budget which has allocated $14 million for Oakland community organizations, small businesses, public safety, and transitional housing. “For 75 years, Fairyland has given Oakland’s children a place to imagine what’s possible. I still remember bringing my sons here, and today we’re making sure the next generation gets that same magic. This $5 million is a proud victory for Oakland because every dollar we put into community spaces comes back to us in the children they raise,” said Mayor Lee. Children’s Fairyland has been a vital part of Oakland’s culture since opening in 1950. As the park that pioneered children’s entertainment in this country, Fairyland forever changed the landscape of “family fun” as it is known today. Children’s Fairyland is ten acres of green space on the shores of Lake Merritt, designed for outdoor play and low-tech, high-touch hands-on learning. It is a rare and increasingly precious resource for children. The $5 million allocation will fund numerous initiatives within Fairyland’s strategic capital investment plan, including essential infrastructure and facility upgrades. Fairyland CEO Miller describes the funding as foundational, rather than final. “This funding is a launchpad, not a landing place. We have much more work to do to create the Fairyland of tomorrow. We’re deeply grateful to Governor Newsom, Mayor Lee, and our State of California partners for recognizing what Fairyland means to this community, to Oakland, and to the entire Bay Area. We are laying the groundwork for Fairyland’s financial sustainability so we can continue to be a safe and inclusive environment for playing and learning, where children build critical literacy skills and grow both socially and emotionally,” said Miller. The state funding is a commitment to ensure the 76-year-old iconic and beloved Oakland destination remains a safe, vibrant, and accessible oasis for generations to come. It also signals a broader shift underway at Fairyland. College Essay Revision Reset By Steph Szczepanek You’ve read your college essay so many times that the words are beginning to blur together. Now what? When you’re deep in the final revision stage, simply rereading the essay again and again becomes counterproductive. Try this instead: 1. Take a real break. Step away from the essay for a day or two if your deadline allows. Work on another part of your application, go for a walk, spend time with friends, or focus on something completely unrelated. The goal is to interrupt your familiarity with the piece. When you return, you are more likely to read the essay as a new reader would, rather than seeing the version that already exists in your head. 2. Change the format. Print it out, change the font, or read it on a different device. A new format can make familiar writing feel unfamiliar enough for you to notice problems. 3. Read it aloud. Listen for sentences that feel awkward, repetitive, overly long, or unlike your natural voice. If you stumble while reading, the sentence may need attention. Remember, the college essay is a particular style of writing — it should sound like you. Reading aloud can help you remember what actually sounds natural, like a person — not a textbook or a résumé. 4. Revise one layer at a time. Don’t try to fix everything in one pass. Read once for the overall story and structure, once for specific details, once for sentence clarity, and once for grammar and spelling. Working in layers makes revision less chaotic. It also helps you recognize when a particular part of the process is complete. 5. Ask a fresh reader a focused question. Instead of asking, “Is it good?” try: “What do you learn about me from this essay?” “Where did you feel most engaged?” “Was anything confusing or unnecessary?” Feedback is most useful when it shows you the effect your writing is having. The purpose of revision is not to make the perfect essay — there is no such thing. You don’t want to polish your essay until it sounds impersonal or nothing like you. Instead, a strong college essay offers a focused glimpse of who you are: how you notice, think, respond, question, change, or care. Revision helps that glimpse become clearer. articles.text: This summer, Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), under the direction of Music Director David Ramadanoff, embarked on a nine-day concert tour of Finland and Sweden. YPSO performed at Sibelius Hall in Lahti and the Helsinki Music Centre in Finland, and at the Filadelfia Convention Centre Concert Hall in Stockholm. The concert program featured works by American composers William Grant Still, Aaron Copland and Samuel Barber, along with Finnish composer Jean Sibelius’s Symphony No. 1. Bet ween per for mances, the young musicians explored Helsinki, the UNESCO World Heritage site of Suomenlinna and the historic town of Porvoo before traveling overnight by ferry across the Baltic Sea to Stockholm. In Sweden, they visited Stockholm City Hall, home of the Nobel Prize banquet, Gamla Stan, the Royal Palace, the Vasa Museum, and Drottningholm Palace, combining their performances with the history and culture of Finland and Sweden. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team lost to Western Alameda County Conference rivals, Bishop O’Dowd, 3-1 on Thursday, October 8 at Binks Rawlings Gym. The result brings the Highlanders’ record to 14-10 overall and 3-4 against league competition. With just three matches remaining on the schedule, the Highlanders are looking to fine tune some final things before the North Coast Section tournament on October 27 or 28. “We’ve got a lot of little things to work on. We need better judgment in certain situations and have a lot of work to do on blocking. We also need the girls to be on the same page on defensive adjustments, but they are growing,” co-head coach Mike Glass said. “The biggest thing to tune up is just our connections to each other, finding spots on the court, finding ways to get kills, and also just working on our defensive setup. Sometimes it’s hard to do that with a team that’s so new,” junior libero Allyson Huynh mentioned. Against the Dragons, Piedmont had a strong second set to win by a dominant score of 25-15. Junior middle Lucia Dorsey was instrumental during the set with three blocks and two kills. However, Bishop O’Dowd started rotating away from her in the third and fourth sets. “In the second set, Lucia took over getting multiple blocks, she made a big difference. But credit to the O’Dowd staff, they made some really good adjustments,” Glass said. Despite the loss, there was a nice crowd on hand for the Highlanders’ benefit to send proceeds to The Cancer League to fight breast cancer. Huynh led setting up the night. “It meant so much to me. It was a lot of work and the student section really showed up for us. We’re raising money for such a good cause. Volleyball is such an exciting sport, I really hope the students who came today really noticed that,” Huynh said. Staff Photos Lucia Dorsey (13) celebrates scoring a point against Bishop O’Dowd after recording one of her five blocks on the night Allyson Huynh (4) celebrates a point in front of Piedmont’s students’ section. Mia Bechtel sets up a spike for Charlotte Bailey. Match Recap Piedmont won one game 25-15, and lost three, 25-18, 25-22, and 25-15. There were five total lead changes in the first set, including the Highlanders holding leads at 6-5 and 10-9. The Dragons took over at 11-10 and ever relinquished their advantage. In Piedmont’s second-set win, they scored the first six points of the set and lead 8-1 early on. BOD inched closer to cut the deficit to 9-5, but PHS went on a 5-0 run with two kills by Olivia Bailey, one by Maika Ting, and an ace by Mia Bechtel. Both teams traded points for the remainder of the set, with PHS maintaining an eight-point lead through much of it. At 21-14, PHS closed with four of the final five points with two kills by Ting and a block by Bailey. In the third set, Piedmont led 2-0 to start by O’Dowd took over at 3-2 and never gave back the lead. Down 10-5, the Highlanders cut the lead to one multiple times, including at 23-22 – but Piedmont couldn’t overtake and two consecutive offensive errors closed the set for O’Dowd. The visitors never trailed in the fourth set, but Piedmont hung tight until around 13-10 when O’Dowd went on an 8-2 scoring run to lead 21-12. They closed with four of the final seven points. Final stats: Ting had 13 kills, one ace and six digs. Olivia Stevens had six kills, five aces, 11 digs and three assists. Dorsey had three kills, three digs, and five blocks. Sofia Meyer had three kills, one dig and one assist. Bailey had two kills and two blocks. Fiona Olsen had two kills. Nora Trombi had two kills. Corina Vora had two kills, five digs and 20 assists. Dando had one kill and two digs. Huynh had 17 digs and three assists. Bechtel had one ace, four digs and six assists. Sarina Hill had four aces. articles.text: Highlanders split matches at Monterey Invitational Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team won three of its last five matches, bringing their record to 9-10 overall with just two matches left in their regular season. The Highlanders beat Castro Valley 10-9 in a Western Alameda County Conference battle at the Piedmont Pool on Tuesday, October 6, while they won two of four matches at the Monterey Invitational Tournament on Friday and Saturday, October 9-10. At the tournament, Piedmont beat host school Pacific Grove 15-9 on the opening day but followed with a 14-0 loss to Santa Cruz. The next day, they lost 19-5 to Carmel, and beat league rivals Bishop O’Dowd 14-11. Piedmont’s final match of the regular season will be hosting O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 20. It marks as a precursor to the start of the WACC Tournament on Tuesday, October 27. 10-9 over Castro Valley PHS opened with a 2-0 lead through the first quarter with goals by Rylan Patty and Walker Wilson. The Highlanders then landed three straight goals in the second quarter by Patty, Henry Stein, and Wilson to lead 5-0 with 1:14 left. The Trojans scored once before halftime to make it 5-1, but went on a four-goal run in the third quarter to tie it at 5-5 with 1:53 remaining. From there, Stein scored with 49 seconds left, but CV tied it again with four seconds remaining. In the fourth quarter, Piedmont found its rhythm again with three straight goals. Stein scored backto-back at 6:50 and 6:01, while Patty made it 9-6 with 4:56 left. After a CV goal, Stein made it 10-7 with 3:49 on the clock. articles.text: Staff Photos Ella Ruthven won in three sets at No. 1 singles against Justin Siena, avenging a loss from last year’s NCS Individual Tournament. It was a dominant 6-1 win for Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team over Justin Siena in Napa on Wednesday, October 7. The result improves Piedmont’s record to 10-4 overall with five matches left in the regular season. The Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament is on November 6. “We traveled for an hour and arrived in that very hot Napa weather and played some glorious tennis,” coach Jim Landes said. The Highlanders look ahead to a critical league match against Alameda today, October 14, in a battle that could determine the fate of the 2026 regular season champion. It marks the first of two matches against the Hornets, with the second being the season-finale on October 28. Against the Braves, Piedmont won three of four singles matches and swept all three doubles. “All three of our doubles teams got off the court quickly without the loss of a set,” Landes said. At singles, sophomore Ella Ruthven had a big three-set win at the No. 1 spot by scores of 6-1, 1-6, 10-6. She defeated Lyla Hogan, who beat Ruthven 6-4, 6-2 in last year’s Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament. “Ella’s win against Lyla Hogan avenged a straight set loss in last season’s NCS Individual, showing the improvement Ella’s has made this year. She was able to control most of the points with good direction on her groundstrokes and varied spin, speed and height of her shots,” Landes said. Also winning at singles was Faith Chin at No. 2 in straight sets, 6-3, 6-2. Maddy Huynh won 6-3, 6-3 at No. 3, while Leela Sivakumar fell in three sets at No. 4 by scores of 1-6, 6-4, 10-8. “Leela played very well but suffered a little more in the heat but still almost pulled out a very good three-set match. Our two other singles players, Faith Chin and Maddy Huyhn, both dominated their opponents and won in straight sets,” Landes said. At doubles, Emma Chan and Chiara Silvio won handily at the No. 1 spot, 6-1, 6-3. Ella Thomasson and Katie Pham featured at No. 2, winning a close first set before handling the second, 7-5, 6-3. At No. 3 was Paige Chin and Layla Reed-Miguel, shutting out their opponent in the second set of a 6-2, 6-0 victory. In a game that nearly ended in a tie, Piedmont High’s junior varsity football team fell 20-12 to the visiting Arroyo Dons by way of a last-second Hail Mary that turned a 12-12 deadlock into a loss. Penalties, fumbles, and a costly interception kept the offense behind the sticks all night, while the defense missed an uncharacteristically high amount of tackles. Even so, the team was tied with eight seconds left against a gritty Arroyo squad. Lev Kuluva put the team on the board in the first quarter, scoring the first touchdown of his career on a rollout Z reverse. He juked the safety and raced 71 yards to the house, showing off the speed he gained on the track team last year. That score marked the first time since 2024 a touchdown was scored on the reverse for the JV Highlanders. In the third quarter, Will Dietrich hauled in a 60 yard interception returned for a touchdown. But Arroyo answered with two straight touchdowns to even the at 12-12. With eight seconds left in the game, the Dons hurled a desperation pass to the end zone, leading to one of their receivers coming down for the catch to leave Piedmont’s JV squad stunned. Defensively, Ernie Hildreth had a strong day with a huge stop to cause a turnover on downs at their own 10 yard line with a ferocious tackle. Robby Koch also recorded an interception, marking his second in two straight games. Ozem Fitzgerald also had a nice game, shedding blocks and racking up six tackles at defensive end. On offense, the team stuck to its trap and toss plays, and the backs combined for about 100 yards, averaging over five yards per carry. The team finished with about 200 total yards, but turnovers and penalties held them to 12 points. Hildreth also ran for about 80 yards, including four carries of at least 10 yards. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team got back in the win column on Friday, October 9 at Witter Field, beating the visiting Arroyo Dons 31-20 in their Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division opener. The result improves Piedmont’s record to 2-4 overall with four games to play. It was a strong second half for the Highlanders after going into the break in a 14-14 deadlock, outscoring the Dons 21-6 in the second half. “From a coaching perspective, it shouldn’t have been that close. They were on an inside run, I took it upon myself to grab the ball. I just wanted to make a huge play and show how I can support this team,” Mafi said of the plays. For Mafi, their September 25 game against Moreau was the first of his varsity career, taking a full year to recover from a torn ACL he suffered on September 19 of last year against Aragon. “Coming back from an injury is truly a blessing. It happened last year against Aragon after forcing a fumble. Coming off this injury, I want to thank my mom and my dad for having my support. They truly mean everything to me. Just being back is truly amazing, and I have to thank the Lord and my parents for having my back,” Mafi said. The result marks the end of a three-game skid for the Highlanders, putting together one of their most complete performances thus far. “Our execution came back, we did everything right. The series featured a 19-yard reception by Mateo Long on 3rd-and-15, and capped off with a 14-yard touchdown by Long on a screen play to the left side to make it 14-14. The Dons scored on its next possession to take a 14-7 lead with 10:20 left in the second quarter. But PHS came right back to score on its next drive on a 76-yard series on eight plays. Photo courtesy of San Francisco Museum of Modern Art The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) will turn its rooftop sculpture garden into a Korean-pop dance party Thursday, October 15, featuring live performances. “Rooftop Radio: K-pop” will take place from 5:30 to 9 p.m. in the sculpture garden on the museum’s fifth floor. K-pop, short for Korean popular music, encompasses a range of musical styles but is known internationally for elaborate choreography and highly visual performances. The genre has become a major part of American pop culture, with groups such as BTS and BLACKPINK reaching the U.S. mainstream through chart success, sold-out concerts and appearances on American television. SFMOMA’s event will feature sets by Bay Area DJs CAZU, AyumiPlease and Peter Lo, along with performances by local K-pop cover groups Groobeu, K-Pop-Up, Homeground Dance and ECLIPSE. Sassi Fran, a San Franciscobased drag performer and co-founder of K-Pop-Up, will host the performances. The evening also will include a photo booth, toploader decorating and activities from Kloud K-Pop, a South Bay K-pop store. Food and drinks will be available for purchase. The 21-and-over event is part of SFMOMA’s Rooftop Radio series, the museum’s after-hours events combining live music, DJ sets, food, drinks, and late-access to museum galleries. articles.text: Haines Galler y at San Francisco’s Fort Mason presents “250 Years, Indigenous Futures,” a group exhibition featuring work by eight Native American artists. The exhibition features Victoria Grace Canby, Jordan Ann Craig, Sky Hopinka, Brad Kahlhamer, Terran Last Gun, Jamie Okuma, Wendy Red Star and Keith Secola. The artists work across painting, drawing, sculpture, photography and film. The works draw from a wide range of sources, including Piikani painted lodges, Northern Cheyenne beadwork, the 1969- 71 occupation of Alcatraz Island by the Indians of All Tribes, the annual Crow Fair, horror films and archival photography. Among the artists featured is Marin-based Victoria Grace Canby, whose new works on paper depict the Three Sisters — corn, beans and squash — as a model of resilience, healing and collective care. Jordan Ann Craig’s paintings combine references to Northern Cheyenne beadwork and quillwork with the work of modernist painter Agnes Martin. S k y H o p i n k a’s f i l m “Sunf lower Siege Engine” connects the occupation of Alcatraz with Cahokia Mounds in Illinois, while Brad Kahlhamer’s “Pima Air + Space” features birds, horses and masked figures rendered in acrylic, ink and pencil on a bedsheet. Terran Last Gun created a series of works inspired by the “Chiaxxúapilake (Fifty)” by Wendy Red Star. geometric designs of Piikani painted lodges, while Jamie Okuma’s “Of Love and Sacrifice: Motherhood” combines intricate Payómkawichum (Luiseño) beadwork with imagery from the 2018 horror film “Suspiria.” The exhibition takes its title from the writings of Standing Rock Sioux historian Philip J. Deloria and his colleagues, who have argued for understanding Native peoples through “the lens of futurity.” The exhibition similarly considers Indigenous creativity and knowledge as active forces shaping contemporary life and the future. Haines Gallery, a resident of Fort Mason since 2022, is dedicated to providing a platform for emerging and internationally established artists from Africa, Asia, Europe, the Middle East, North and South America. “250 Years, Indigenous Futures” is on view now through Saturday, November 7, 2026 at Haines Gallery located in Building C, on the first floor of the Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture. Admission is free. Visit https://fortmason.org/ event/haines-gallery-250-yearsindigenous-futures/2026-09-22/ to learn more.

articles.text: Cal Performances will present the West Coast premiere of South African artist William Kentridge’s theater production “The Head & the Load” November 12 through 15 at the Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts in Oakland. The multidisciplinary work examines the history of more than 2 million Africans who fought and died during World War I. The production combines dance, projections, speech, song, shadow play, costumes and music to explore the effects of colonialism and war. Directed and conceived by Kentridge, the production features choreography by Gregory Maqoma and music composed by Philip Miller and Thuthuka Sibisi. Its score combines traditional Af rican songs, European compositions, war chants and percussion. The libretto draws on texts from anticolonial writers, Dada poets and Setswana proverbs. The production takes its title from a Ghanaian proverb: “The head and the load are the troubles of the neck.” Kentridge has described the work as an effort to document the experiences of Black participants whose contributions to the war have often been overlooked. “The Head & the Load” premiered in 2018 at Tate Modern in London, followed by performances at New York City’s Park Avenue Armory that year. The Oakland performances mark its West Coast premiere. A 180- foot stage will be constructed in the Kaiser Center’s arena to accommodate the production. The performances also launch a five-season Cal Performances initiative to present a different interdisciplinar y work by Kentridge each season. The organization previously presented his “Sibyl” in 2023 and “The Great Yes, The Great No” in 2025. Kentridge will participate in a free pre-performance conversation with Debarati Sanyal, director of UC Berkeley’s Center for Interdisciplinary Critical Inquiry, from 6 to 7 p.m. November 13. The discussion will address the production’s historical context and its relationship to the season’s Illuminations theme. The event is free to ticket holders for that evening’s performance. Performances are scheduled for 7:30 p.m. November 12-14 and 3 p.m. November 15 at the Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts, 10 10th St., Oakland. Tickets are available at calperformances.org or by calling the box office at 510-642-9988. Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts in Oakland. Photo by Scott Hergis

articles.text: The Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek will host a presentation on creating beefriendly gardens Wednesday, November 4, led by Claudia Cruse of UC Berkeley’s Urban Bee Lab. The 11 a.m. to noon program, “Gardening for Native Bees,” will cover California’s native bee species, the plants they prefer and ways to create gardens that provide food and habitat throughout the year. The Urban Bee Lab at UC Berkeley has studied bee diversity and relationships between bees and plants across California since 1987. Its research has identified about 90 bee species in East Bay residential areas, most of them native to the state, according to the garden’s event description. The lab also has developed an experimental bee garden at UC Berkeley to demonstrate how residential landscapes can support native bees and other pollinators. The program will take place at the Ruth Bancroft Garden, a nonprofit botanical garden and nursery at 1552 Bancroft Road. The 3.5-acre garden is known for its collection of droughttolerant plants, including cacti, succulents, aloes and agaves, and offers educational programs, tours and gardening resources. articles.text: Celebrate Dia de los Muertos at OMCA with music, dance, food and art. The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) will host its 32nd annual Día de los Muertos Community Celebration from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. October 25, featuring music, dance, art, food and community-created altars honoring the dead. The event will include an opening procession, traditional and contemporary ofrendas, or offering altars, along with hands-on crafts, performances, demonstrations and an artisanal market. A formal welcome is scheduled for noon. A special ofrenda, “Sanando Corazones, Healing Hearts,” is on view at the museum now through November 29. Created by members of OMCA’s volunteer Día de los Muertos Committee, the installation uses the heart as a symbol of love, remembrance and support for East Bay families who have lost loved ones, as well as those affected by natural disasters and warfare. “Though our ofrendas to our dead traditionally contain items that represent spirituality, love, and life experiences, we chose to add the image of a heart as a symbol to express our heartfelt sadness and support to all East Bay families who have experienced the loss of a loved one,” the OMCA Día de los Muertos Ofrenda Installation Photo courtesy of OMCA Subcommittee wrote in a press release. The subcommittee also dedicates this year’s ofrenda “to all who died this year due to the disasters created by nature and warfare.” Visitors may bring picnic blankets, low-back lawn chairs, sun protection, and layers or a light jacket to help stay comfortable throughout the celebration. Guests are also welcome to bring their own food and non-alcoholic beverages to enjoy during the day. Food and beverages will be available for purchase. Tickets are available at museumca.org.

articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group met on Monday, October 5 in the Community Hall to discuss their September book, Freezing Order, by Bill Browder. The book picks up after Browder’s previous bestseller, Red Notice, and follows the 2009 prison death of Browder’s Russian lawyer, Sergei Magnitsky. Magnitsky was tortured and killed after uncovering a $230 million state tax refund fraud scheme in Russia. Browder and his investigative team tracked the stolen funds as they moved out of Russia through Cyprus, the Baltics, Western Europe, and the Americas. The investigation revealed that Russian President Vladimir Putin was a primary financial beneficiary of the laundered funds. A s i nt e r n at ion a l l aw enforcement agencies began freezing the tracked assets, Putin and his associates targeted Browder. He faced international process servers, honey traps, Inter pol ar rest war rants, murdered allies, and intense lobbying by high-profile Western lawyers and politicians hired to undermine him. The book argues that Browder’s relentless campaign to expose Putin’s hidden wealth directly motivated the Kremlin’s interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election. When the Piedmont reading group did a “thumbs up, thumbs down, thumbs sideways” vote on how they felt about the book. Many in the group gave an enthusiastic “thumbs up,” a handful gave “thumbs sideways,” and one gave a “thumbs down.” Then two people who liked the book shared what they liked, followed by two who thought it was just so-so. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers honor Piedmont’s World Wars fallen heroes It was another warm Piedmont day on Oct. 7 when 44 members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group and three of their K-9 best friends gathered at the Exedra for their weekly walk. Piedmont Recreation Commissioner Nancy Beninati and Solene Francois, who is from France and working in Piedmont this year, walked with the group for the first time. Sherry Jacobs led the walk. Her theme was “Piedmont WWI Fallen Heroes.” Seven young Piedmont men were killed in World War I, and Sherry wanted the group to see where they lived and remember them. Sherry started off by leading the walkers up Mountain Avenue to 21 Dormidera Ave., where Thomas Edward Graves lived with his parents. Graves, a U.S. Army lieutenant, was 23 years old and an aviation instructor in Washington, D.C., when his airplane crashed during a preliminary test. The group then went over to Vista Avenue and the Piedmont Veterans Memorial Building. The city’s original marble World War I Memorial sits underneath a set of tall redwood trees to the right of the building’s entrance. The memorial was designed by architect Albert Farr and dedicated on Armistice Day, Nov. 11, 1921. The names inscribed on it are Egbert William Beach, Henry Augustus Butters, Otto Julius Carlsen, Hunter McClure, Frank Jay Field, Thomas Edward Graves, and Carl Castlemayne Jones. It originally stood in a grove of redwood trees east of Piedmont’s commercial center, where Memorial Day observances were held, and California Gov. Earl Warren visited it on Armistice Day in 1943. It was most likely moved to its present spot when the Veterans Building was built in 1953. Up the steps to the building’s entrance is an Honor Roll with the names of all the service members from Piedmont who lost their lives in our country’s four major 20th-century conflicts: the seven men from World War I, 50 from World War II and six from the Korean War. Six more from the Vietnam War were later added to the plaque. The walkers noted how large Piedmont’s World War II loss was. The 50 young men were about 0.51% of the city’s 1940 population of 9,866, compared with 0.31% nationally, or about one in 20 of Piedmont’s fightingage men. The walkers took their group photo in front of the World War I Memorial and then went down to Bonita Avenue and up to 323 and 319 Bonita Ave., the homes of Henry Augustus Butters’ family members. Butters was a second lieutenant in the British Army and was killed during the Battle of the Somme on Aug. 31, 1916. He was 24. Unlike the other men on Piedmont’s memorial, he served in the British Army rather than with American forces, and he died before the United States entered the war in April 1917. The group continued up Bonita to 128 Bonita Ave., the home of Hunter McClure of the U.S. Army, who lived in Piedmont with his aunt, Mrs. G. H. Harris. A November 1921 Oakland Tribune account said he was killed in the Argonne on Sept. 26, 1918, the opening day of the MeuseArgonne Offensive. The walkers then made their way to 906 Rose Ave., the home of Mr. and Mrs. Fred Jones, whose son, Carl Castlemayne Jones of the U.S. Army, was 26 years old when he was killed in the Argonne on Sept. 27, 1918, as American troops attacked heavily defended German positions. The Walking on Wednesdays group gathers at the Piedmont World War I Memorial on Oct. 7. articles.text: Part One Tucked between Burgundy and the Swiss border in eastern France, the Jura wine region is one of the country’s smallest and most distinctive wine-producing areas. Its rolling hills, limestone-rich soils and cool continental climate provide the setting for wines that have increasingly captured the attention of sommeliers, collectors and adventurous drinkers. Stretching along the foothills of the Jura Mountains, the region is home to picturesque villages, historic cellars and vineyards that reflect centuries of winemaking tradition. Its principal wine towns include Arbois, Château-Chalon and L’Étoile, each offering a glimpse into the region’s rich cultural heritage. Jura is perhaps best known for vin jaune, or “yellow wine,” an unusual specialty made predominantly from the Savagnin grape. After fermentation, the wine ages for at least six years and three months in barrels without being topped up, allowing a protective veil of yeast to develop. The result is a complex, golden wine with distinctive notes of walnuts, spices and dried fruit. Yet Jura’s appeal extends well beyond this celebrated style. Winemakers produce fresh, mineral-driven whites from Chardonnay and Savagnin, elegant reds from Poulsard and Trousseau, and Crémant du Jura, a traditional-method sparkling wine. The region is also renowned for vin de paille, a luscious, sweet wine made from grapes dried before fermentation. Another local treasure is the traditional oxidative wine style, which develops nutty, savory flavors through prolonged exposure to oxygen. Alongside these historic techniques, a new generation of growers is embracing organic and biodynamic viticulture, bringing renewed international attention to Jura. The region’s gastronomy is equally compelling. Local wines pair naturally with Comté, the celebrated mountain cheese, as well as freshwater fish, poultry, fondue and creamy regional dishes. Although Jura remains relatively under the radar compared with neighboring Burgundy, its individuality is precisely its strength. For travelers seeking authentic French wine culture, unspoiled landscapes and bottles with a compelling sense of place, Jura offers a rewarding discovery. articles.text: Alongside the five members of the Piedmont Board of Education sit student representatives, providing a voice for the student body where decisions are made. This fall, those two students are PHS junior Diego Branneria and MHS junior Corinne Minor. “I applied because I thought it’d be a really good opportunity to get more involved with our community, and I was also curious how the Board works,” Minor said. “I thought it was a good opportunity for me to branch out and learn how to speak in front of a lot of people.” According to the PUSD Website, Student Board members are elected in a process that involves an initial application screening, and once the Board has chosen candidates, a student election. “I applied because I think it’s super important, especially in Piedmont, that we hold our decision makers accountable,” Branneria said. “I think we also are a really unique district where we have a ton of strength, but there are also a lot of ways that we can better support our students.” The role of Student Board members involves participation in discussions at Board Meetings and updating the Board on happenings at Piedmont schools. The Student Board members vote on issues but their votes are not counted, Minor said. “I really hope student board members can get a position to actually vote and have our votes be counted, because I know they do that in Berkeley and Oakland, but not in Piedmont yet,” Minor said. Branneria said that one of the main issues he sees with Piedmont schools right now is the emphasis on test scores and academic performance over student wellbeing. “I think we need to do a better job making sure that Piedmont kids are being set up for success, not just to take the SAT once they get into high school, but to actually enjoy their experience and learn things that they really want to learn about,” Branneria said. “We should be prioritizing student well-being over academic excellence, because we can do both.” Branneria also said he thinks teacher salaries in Piedmont can be improved. “I hope that we can make progress in supporting our teachers more, because I don’t think that the community understands that Piedmont does not have a competitive teacher salary,” Branneria said. “We’ve had five chemistry teachers in the past six years. This isn’t a coincidence.” Minor and Branneria will serve on the School Board for just the fall semester, but plan to continue to stay involved after their time on the Board. “There are a lot of things that need work,” Branneria said. “There’s more than just ‘Piedmont is a great school district.’ Even though it is.” Julia Stokes is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student writer intern for the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: Honors English was recently added to Piedmont High School’s list of course offerings for sophomores, to a chorus of mixed opinions. The addition is part of a recent push to increase the presence of weighted classes in the school’s curriculum. While this rigor is supposed to be an improvement to the school, its effects on students remain unclear. As of today, most students are critical of the addition, finding it stress-inducing and divisive. One junior at Piedmont High believes that the addition of “10th Honors English and Honors MWH is a bad decision. I know sophomores taking weighted classes, even though they technically don’t have to…high achieving students will automatically feel pressured.” She speaks from a place of familiarity, as she is currently enrolled in three AP classes (AP Chem, AP US History, and AP Calculus BC). She has been able to manage her busy schedule through good study habits, but acknowledged that the options have made her feel like she needs to “take an AP in a subject to be ‘good’ at it.” She also noted that she has found herself comparing the number of APs on her schedule to that of others. Another junior agreed with the first student, saying that she felt encouraged to take weighted classes that she is less passionate about so that she could “be on par” with other students. A third student added that it creates “peer pressure.” In a perfect world, a student’s schedule would reflect their interests. Currently, students are taking classes just because they feel like they must, stopping them from engaging with the material fully. This detracts from the reason the classes were added in the first place: creating more learning opportunities. Some students have felt that they were able to learn more from the earlier course offerings. One said that taking the non-honors English and History classes as a sophomore was “completely fine and a very valuable experience.” The same student, now taking both AP US History and Honors English in her junior year, says that while her classes are interesting, the homework is “overwhelming” and sometimes she wishes she had “more time to just think about what [she’s] learning.” Increasing honors offerings earlier seems to accelerate the discontentment, taking away from the value of the course rather than opening more avenues for knowledge. Head-Royce School in Oakland has taken a different approach when it comes to rigor. After COVID, the private school completely phased out APs, and while it still has weighted honors classes, the split is only present in the STEM subjects. Additionally, the school allows seniors to build their schedules from a large list of “senior seminars.” This, in the opinion of many students, allows them to follow their interests rather than outside pressure. One Head-Royce senior, Anaiah Singh, says that getting to build her schedule herself has made her feel “more fulfilled” overall. Pressure will exist everywhere: in high school, in college, and in the workplace. However, it should feel like constructive pressure, especially for growing brains. Students should be taught to stretch themselves out of interest in their subjects, rather than the perceived opinions of peers and college admissions officers. The current shift at Piedmont High puts students in a pressure cooker, risking dissatisfaction and higher risk of burnout. At the end of the day, the decisions of the school board and the reviews of the students themselves will determine the weighted class debate. Mira Sen is a sophomore at Head Royce High School and a student writer intern with the Piedmont Post. website: piedmont-post.com instagram: @thepiedmontpost

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, October 14, 2026 Student Board Members bring new perspectives By Julia Stokes Alongside the five members of the Piedmont Board of Education sit student representatives, providing a voice for the student body where decisions are made. This fall, those two students are PHS junior Diego Branneria and MHS junior Corinne Minor. “I applied because I thought it’d be a really good opportunity to get more involved with our community, and I was also curious how the Board works,” Minor said. “I thought it was a good opportunity for me to branch out and learn how to speak in front of a lot of people.” According to the PUSD Website, Student Board members are elected in a process that involves an initial application screening, and once the Board has chosen candidates, a student election. “I applied because I think it’s super important, especially in Piedmont, that we hold our decision makers accountable,” Branneria said. “I think we also are a really unique district where we have a ton of strength, but there are also a lot of ways that we can better support our students.” The role of Student Board members involves participation in discussions at Board Meetings and updating the Board on happenings at Piedmont schools. The Student Board members vote on issues but their votes are not counted, Minor said. “I really hope student board members can get a position to actually vote and have our votes be counted, because I know they do that in Berkeley and Oakland, but not in Piedmont yet,” Minor said. Branneria said that one of the main issues he sees with Piedmont schools right now is the emphasis on test scores and academic performance over student wellbeing. “I think we need to do a better job making sure that Piedmont kids are being set up for success, not just to take the SAT once they get into high school, but to actually enjoy their experience and learn things that they really want to learn about,” Branneria said. “We should be prioritizing student well-being over academic excellence, because we can do both.” Branneria also said he thinks teacher salaries in Piedmont can be improved. “I hope that we can make progress in supporting our teachers more, because I don’t think that the community understands that Piedmont does not have a competitive teacher salary,” Branneria said. “We’ve had five chemistry teachers in the past six years. This isn’t a coincidence.” Minor and Branneria will serve on the School Board for just the fall semester, but plan to continue to stay involved after their time on the Board. “There are a lot of things that need work,” Branneria said. “There’s more than just ‘Piedmont is a great school district.’ Even though it is.” Julia Stokes is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student writer intern for the Piedmont Post. The average high school GPA in the U.S. rose from 2.6 in 1985 to 3.1 in 2020, according to the National Education Society The Weighted Class Debate By Mira Sen Honors English was recently added to Piedmont High School’s list of course offerings for sophomores, to a chorus of mixed opinions. The addition is part of a recent push to increase the presence of weighted classes in the school’s curriculum. While this rigor is supposed to be an improvement to the school, its effects on students remain unclear. As of today, most students are critical of the addition, finding it stress-inducing and divisive. One junior at Piedmont High believes that the addition of “10th Honors English and Honors MWH is a bad decision. I know sophomores taking weighted classes, even though they technically don’t have to…high achieving students will automatically feel pressured.” She speaks from a place of familiarity, as she is currently enrolled in three AP classes (AP Chem, AP US History, and AP Calculus BC). She has been able to manage her busy schedule through good study habits, but acknowledged that the options have made her feel like she needs to “take an AP in a subject to be ‘good’ at it.” She also noted that she has found herself comparing the number of APs on her schedule to that of others. Another junior agreed with the first student, saying that she felt encouraged to take weighted classes that she is less passionate about so that she could “be on par” with other students. A third student added that it creates “peer pressure.” In a perfect world, a student’s schedule would reflect their interests. Currently, students are taking classes just because they feel like they must, stopping them from engaging with the material fully. This detracts from the reason the classes were added in the first place: creating more learning opportunities. Some students have felt that they were able to learn more from the earlier course offerings. One said that taking the non-honors English and History classes as a sophomore was “completely fine and a very valuable experience.” The same student, now taking both AP US History and Honors English in her junior year, says that while her classes are interesting, the homework is “overwhelming” and sometimes she wishes she had “more time to just think about what [she’s] learning.” Increasing honors offerings earlier seems to accelerate the discontentment, taking away from the value of the course rather than opening more avenues for knowledge. Head-Royce School in Oakland has taken a different Graphic courtesy of The Plaid Press approach when it comes to rigor. After COVID, the private school completely phased out APs, and while it still has weighted honors classes, the split is only present in the STEM subjects. Additionally, the school allows seniors to build their schedules from a large list of “senior seminars.” This, in the opinion of many students, allows them to follow their interests rather than outside pressure. One Head-Royce senior, Anaiah Singh, says that getting to build her schedule herself has made her feel “more fulfilled” overall. Pressure will exist everywhere: in high school, in college, and in the workplace. However, it should feel like constructive pressure, especially for growing brains. Students should be taught to stretch themselves out of interest in their subjects, rather than the perceived opinions of peers and college admissions officers. The current shift at Piedmont High puts students in a pressure cooker, risking dissatisfaction and higher risk of burnout. At the end of the day, the decisions of the school board and the reviews of the students themselves will determine the weighted class debate. Mira Sen is a sophomore at Head Royce High School and a student writer intern with the Piedmont Post. Digger Continued from page 18 an airplane like a madman, Tom Cruise is a damn good actor. He has played memorable, off-kilter characters before, in Magnolia and Tropic Thunder, and Digger Rockwell belongs in that company. The fault isn’t in the themes, either. It’s in how the film was sold. The marketing did the film no favors: the initial trailers sold it as a screwball dark comedy in the vein of the Coen Brothers, built around a familiar threat of a climate catastrophe. But early in the first act, a twist, hidden by the marketing, turns the whole movie on its head. I won’t spoil it here, but the film shifts from a Coen Brothers romp about runaway glaciers into a spiritual successor to Birdman, one focused on the intriguing role satire plays in the current zeitgeist. That rug pull is gutsy and absolutely a big swing, but it is also divisive. Some will applaud the subversion and the fresh take, while others will see it as false advertising and a waste of their hard-earned time and money. I knew the twist going in and was still pleasantly surprised by how it played out over the rest of the film’s 129-minute runtime. That is the real story of Digger. It isn’t a bad movie; it is a hard movie to sell. Asking a mainstream audience to buy a ticket for one film and then sit through a different one was always going to be a gamble at this price tag, and the opening weekend suggests many moviegoers either sensed the bait-and-switch or simply weren’t interested in the film they ultimately got. Critics have split almost down the middle, and audiences who did turn out have been lukewarm too. I saw it on a Saturday afternoon in a nearly empty theater: seven people, including me, and two of them walked out before the ending. As the credits rolled, an older woman sighed, “Well, that’s two hours I’ll never get back.” I couldn’t have disagreed more with that sentiment. But a big, strange, expensive swing from an Oscar-winning director and arguably still the world’s most bankable movie star is increasingly rare in a multiplex dominated by sequels and superheroes, and that alone makes Digger worth seeing on the big screen, where Iñárritu’s visuals land hardest. Go in knowing it isn’t the movie the trailers promised. Go in for Cruise’s monologue, which is worth the ticket on its own. And go soon, because a film losing this much money won’t stay in theaters long. Years from now, it may well be rediscovered as a cult classic, the way box office disappointments like Blade Runner and Fight Club were. If it is, you’ll be able to say you saw it on the big screen. Digger Rockwell’s granddaddy had it right. Everyone behind Digger went for that triple, then got greedy and tried to stretch it into an inside-the-park home run. The box office numbers show they were thrown out at the plate.
