articles.text: My goal is to ensure that our police have the tools they need to keep our community safe, while carefully evaluating their effectiveness and ensuring they are used responsibly, lawfully, and with appropriate oversight. Adam Hundt (AdamHundt.com) There are legitimate uses for Flock for public safety, but before voting to renew the contract, I would investigate if and how data gathered from Piedmont’s Flock cameras is used. I support public safety measures, but I acknowledge residents’ legitimate privacy concerns. I will ensure these concerns are addressed. When the Piedmont City Council voted to approve Flock cameras, the intent was to monitor stolen or missing vehicles or vehicles used to commit crimes in and around the city. Piedmont’s safety cameras have helped reduce crime, including larceny/theft and motor vehicle theft, which are the city’s highest crime categories (based on a 5-year average, 2019-2024). Piedmont works with Flock to provide a public ALPR Transparency Portal that shares information regarding camera operations. My professional experience at technology companies is helpful in reviewing the privacy safeguards Piedmont must impose on Flock data. If elected to Council, I will follow up on the suggestion that police department staffing be prioritized. In the 2025-2026 budget year, the city projects to be under its approved budget for regular and part-time salaries and 50% over its approved budget on overtime salaries. Tom Ramsey, Incumbent (Vote4TomRamsey.com) California’s anti-bias rules and the Brown Act discourage me from deciding on a vote before a public hearing, so I’ll wait to review the contract and have a public discussion before answering the voting question. This topic is important, though. I support the use of cameras and ALPR technology and think of this issue in three parts: Safety and civil liberties: Cameras and license plate reader technology help keep our town safe, but safeguarding resident privacy is non-negotiable. Transparency: The Piedmont Police Department was the first law enforcement agency in the nation to launch an ALPR Transparency Portal. This public resource tracks data and lists each external agency that has access. Guardrails: Our system does not use facial recognition; data is encrypted, automatically deleted on a 30-day rolling timeline, and is owned 100% by the city. State laws restrict sharing to legitimate law enforcement purposes only. While we have guardrails in place, we need to be diligent in updating our practices and policies to keep pace with technology, remain transparent, and keep the public’s trust. Bill Reichle (ReichleForPiedmont.com) Automatic License Plate Readers (ALPR) cameras are one tool the Piedmont Police Department uses to aid investigations. Piedmont has used this technology with success since 2014, and the current contract runs through 2028. Flock is one vendor, and other competitors offer similar ALPR technology. Flock cameras have lately become a symbol for society’s unease with our eroding sense of privacy. Smartphones and connected devices have technology that tracks our locations, conversations, communications, and consumer-spending habits, while ALPR is limited to capturing license plates. Nevertheless, the disquiet is real, and there have been alarming incidents of misuse of ALPR data from around the country. It is right to be concerned and demand oversight and accountability. Any decision to issue or renew a contract for ALPRs would require listening to Piedmont residents to fully understand their concerns, an analysis by PPD of the costbenefit of this tool, discussing the opportunity cost of forgoing other tools, a gap analysis of features and safeguards, and a competitive analysis to see what features competitors can offer. This analysis would need to include cybersecurity protections vendors offer to prevent and report on unauthorized access. Sunny Bostrom-Fleming As the person who was instrumental in inspiring the installation of these security devices, I’m acutely aware of how these devices have proven to be effective. They’ve apprehended individuals driving through our Piedmont streets day and night who have warrants from other cities and states for previous crimes. I am totally in favor of continuing with Flock. However, we need to review the 150 agencies receiving this sensitive information, because safeguarding personal information remains a very high priority. We don’t have enough information on the current recipients to determine who should be added or subtracted from the list already receiving our sensitive information. The Flock collected information should be shared with law enforcement, both local and national, and certainly not for commercial purposes or by agencies that resell information. We should take a good look at increasing camera coverage in our schools, playgrounds, and parks. The Dearing Memorial Art Project, which cost $400,000, needs camera coverage inside and out to discourage it from becoming a homeless shelter, illegal drug dispensary, toilet, a graffiti magnet, and other criminal activity.
